items.name: Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse
items.summary: Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse (1504–1567), nicknamed 'the Magnanimous,' was a German nobleman and champion of the Protestant Reformation, one of the most important early Protestant rulers in Germany. Despite imperfect education, he developed rapidly as a statesman. He embraced Protestantism in 1524 and helped suppress the German Peasants' War by defeating Thomas Müntzer at the Battle of Frankenhausen. Philip organized the church in Hesse according to Protestant principles, leading to the founding of the University of Marburg in 1527. He contributed to the Regensburg religious colloquy in 1541 and successfully secured imperial permission for the university. On his death, his territories were divided between his four sons.

items.name: Robert Bunsen
items.summary: Robert Wilhelm Eberhard Bunsen was a German chemist born in 1811. He studied with famous scientists like Gauss and Liebig before becoming a professor. Bunsen developed the Bunsen burner with his assistant Peter Desaga, creating a very hot and clean flame used in labs today. Working with Gustav Kirchhoff, he discovered two new elements: caesium in 1860 and rubidium in 1861. They invented a prototype spectroscope to study the colors of heated elements. Bunsen also did important work in photochemistry and organic arsenic chemistry, leading to effective antidotes for poisoning. His discoveries brought him wide acclaim and an award named after him.

items.name: Emil von Behring
items.summary: Emil von Behring was a German physiologist who revolutionized medicine by developing serum therapy against diphtheria and tetanus. Born in 1854, he studied medicine in Berlin and later worked with Robert Koch. In 1890, he and Kitasato Shibasaburō discovered that injecting toxins into animals could produce antitoxins to cure these diseases. After optimizing the process, successful human treatments began in 1894. Behring founded a company to produce these treatments and became a professor at the University of Marburg. He was awarded the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901 for his work, earning him the title 'saviour of children' as diphtheria was a major cause of child death.

items.name: Jacob Grimm
items.summary: Jacob Ludwig Karl Grimm (1785–1863) was a German author, linguist, and folklorist. He co-authored Grimms' Fairy Tales with his brother Wilhelm, collecting folktales from people and manuscripts. Together, they also published German Legends. Grimm formulated Grimm's law of linguistics and co-authored the monumental Deutsches Wörterbuch, a German language dictionary started in 1838. This dictionary remains a standard reference work today. He also published legal compilations like Weisthümer, studying rural German legal traditions. His work influenced the western world through his fairy tales and linguistic discoveries.

items.name: Hannah Arendt
items.summary: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was a German and American historian and philosopher, one of the most influential political theorists of the twentieth century. Born to a Jewish family in Linden, she studied at the University of Marburg under Martin Heidegger, where she engaged in a romantic affair. She obtained her doctorate in philosophy at the University of Heidelberg in 1929, with a dissertation on Love and Saint Augustine. Her works cover topics like wealth, power, and totalitarianism. Arendt was briefly imprisoned by the Gestapo in 1933 for illegal research into antisemitism.

items.summary: Baroness Gertrud von Le Fort (1876–1971) was a German writer born in Minden, the daughter of a Prussian colonel. She studied in Heidelberg, Marburg, and Berlin before making her home in Bavaria. Her career began with editing Ernst Troeltsch's posthumous work in 1925, followed by her conversion to Roman Catholicism. She published over 20 books, including the novella The Song at the Scaffold, which inspired Georges Bernanos' Dialogues des Carmélites. This work formed the basis for Francis Poulenc's 1956 opera. Le Fort won the Gottfried-Keller Prize in 1952 and was nominated by Hermann Hesse for the Nobel Prize.

items.name: Alfred Wegener
items.summary: Alfred Wegener (1880–1930) was a German scientist who pioneered polar research and meteorology. He proposed the continental drift hypothesis in 1912, suggesting continents slowly move across Earth. His work later supported plate tectonics. Wegener led expeditions to Greenland, where he and his brother pioneered weather balloon use. He died in 1930 during a polar expedition, buried in a mausoleum in the ice. His ability to explain complex science made him a valued lecturer. He published nearly 20 papers before his death, exploring new scientific frontiers.

items.name: Boris Pasternak
items.summary: Boris Pasternak (1890–1960) was a Russian poet, novelist, and translator who began composing at age 13. He studied philosophy in Germany before returning to Russia to join the Futurist group. His first book, My Sister, Life, revolutionized Russian poetry in 1922. He wrote the famous novel Doctor Zhivago, which was smuggled out of the USSR and published in 1957. Pasternak won the 1958 Nobel Prize in Literature but declined it due to Soviet pressure. His son eventually accepted the award in 1989. Pasternak also translated works by Shakespeare and Goethe, remaining popular with Russian audiences.
